key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the credit-card autopay-minimum default cut exact-minimum payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt.
methodology: Field experiment on credit card autopay enrollment, six-month follow-up, large cardholder sample.
why_it_matters: Directly tests the brief's core question—whether changing an enrollment default shifts behavior nominally but not the underlying amount—showing behavior change without an outcome improvement, a warning for judging round-up enrollment by sign-up counts alone.
limitations: Domain is credit-card repayment, not a savings sweep, so the direction of desired behavior differs.
Abstract does not give exact debt-reduction confidence intervals.
relevance_reason: Closest available consumer financial-product test of a default/nudge changing enrollment without changing the outcome that matters, matching the brief's amount-vs-enrollment question.

key_finding: Synthesizes literature showing automatic enrollment defaults raise participation but can dampen long-term account engagement, with employees anchoring at low default contribution rates.
methodology: Narrative literature overview of defined-contribution plan design research; abstract-only, no independent estimates.
why_it_matters: Provides a recent survey of the persistence and anchoring findings, useful for calibrating expectations about our multiplier default but drawn entirely from employer-plan evidence.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement setting, not a consumer self-directed app.
A narrative review rather than a systematic synthesis with pooled effect sizes.
relevance_reason: Gives a recent overview of default persistence and anchoring effects, though drawn from the employer-plan literature the brief says needs careful translation.

key_finding: Argues default enrollment raises short-term retirement participation but induces low-contribution inertia, account churn, and passivity that undermine welfare gains unless paired with auto-escalation and reminders.
methodology: Policy discussion article synthesizing prior empirical findings; no new data (abstract-only).
why_it_matters: Reinforces the support team's concern that passive enrollment produces disengaged, low-value participants, and suggests mitigations (auto-escalation, reminders) that could apply to the round-up multiplier design.
limitations: Employer retirement-plan context, not a liquid consumer product.
Very low citation count and narrow venue suggest limited peer scrutiny.
No original data or effect sizes.
relevance_reason: Directly voices the 'passive trap' argument central to the brief's internal debate, even though set in retirement plans.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for when default effects persist, fade, or reverse downstream, driven by the time course of choice, prior preferences, and salience of trade-offs.
methodology: Conceptual/theoretical review synthesizing prior default-effect literature into a research agenda; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the mechanism-level account of exactly the question the brief asks—whether enrollment defaults change durable behavior or fade—useful for predicting which round-up users will disengage and why.
limitations: Theoretical synthesis, not a new empirical estimate.
Not specific to financial products, so predictions must be validated in our setting.
relevance_reason: Directly addresses persistence and downstream default effects in consumer decision-making, the mechanism question underlying the enrollment-vs-disengagement trade-off.

key_finding: Default enrollment in Medicare Part D produces large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is insensitive even to substantial losses from staying in a bad default.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options in a large administrative dataset.
why_it_matters: Shows defaults can persist for a long time and shift real resource allocation, not just nominal enrollment—useful evidence that persistence is possible, but the population and product differ sharply from our liquid savings app.
limitations: Health-insurance setting, not a financial savings product.
Population is low-income Medicare beneficiaries, not self-directed banking-app users.
relevance_reason: Strong general evidence on default persistence and passivity insensitivity, useful by analogy despite the health-insurance setting.

key_finding: Steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from automatic enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation once job turnover, pre-vesting withdrawals, and opt-outs are accounted for; only 40% of auto-escalation defaults are accepted at the first escalation date.
methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job separation, balance withdrawal, and opt-out dynamics.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified rebuttal of the 'defaults will lift enrollment so default everyone in' premise: medium/long-run dynamics erode most of the apparent gain, directly supporting the support team's skepticism.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings.
Abstract gives steady-state estimates but not month-by-month withdrawal timing relevant to a round-up feature.
relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving amounts, which the brief explicitly asked us to test.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment in Germany's public pension raised participation by 23 percentage points among low-income employees, but most affected individuals actively opted out, with the effect size moderated by incentive size and awareness.
methodology: Natural policy experiment using nationwide administrative and survey data on auto-enrollment introduction.
why_it_matters: Quantifies how the default effect's size depends on incentive salience and knowledge of enrollment status—relevant to predicting whether an opt-out round-up default will actually stick once users realize they can leave.
limitations: Public pension for low-income employees, not a self-directed consumer app.
Working paper, not yet peer-reviewed (2026 CESifo).
relevance_reason: Gives an effect-size estimate for opt-out default enrollment and shows heterogeneity by incentive and awareness, informative context for our opt-out design even though the setting is a state pension.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment's participation and contribution gains, replicated at 12 months, attenuate substantially by 36 months, though it still reduces savings inequality; a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a $250 switching cost.
methodology: Analysis of 100+ US retirement plans plus a UK panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's persistence question with a specific horizon comparison (12 vs 36 months), showing the enrollment lift decays—key evidence against assuming a default's headline effect will hold at 6-12 months.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement accounts, not a liquid, self-directed savings feature.
Structural model relies on assumptions about switching costs that may not map to a mobile banking context.
relevance_reason: Best available quantification of default-effect attenuation over the medium run, the exact persistence question the brief raises, despite the pension setting.

key_finding: Across experiments including a 4,207-person five-country European sample, default nudges produced medium-to-large shifts in risk-taking but also lowered users' ratings of the advice/wealth manager, especially when the default was one they refused.
methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative multi-country European sample, testing default framing and presentation effects on investment allocation and perceived advice quality.
why_it_matters: Provides direct European evidence that a default can be perceived as manipulative and damage trust when it's not accepted—precisely the reputational, dark-pattern risk the EU-context brief flags for the entry and level decisions.
limitations: Setting is investment/wealth-management advice rather than a round-up savings sweep specifically.
Effect on trust is a self-reported rating, not behavioral churn or complaints.
relevance_reason: Directly measures the manipulation/trust cost of defaults in a European financial-advice context, matching the brief's concern about dark-pattern perception.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85% at three firms, but roughly 80% of participants accepted both the low default contribution rate and conservative default fund, with half still at the default after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms analyzing 401(k) participation, contribution, and asset accumulation under automatic enrollment.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a preset level anchors most users for years, directly relevant to whether our 1x/2x/5x multiplier default will similarly trap people at whichever level we pre-select.
limitations: Classic employer 401(k) study, not a consumer liquid-savings app.
Predates the mobile app and EU regulatory context the brief asks us to weight more heavily.
relevance_reason: The foundational anchoring result the newer literature responds to, directly on point for the preset-multiplier anchoring question even though set in retirement plans.

key_finding: In 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions, 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost together; adding a lower preset option (15%) to an existing menu captured 69% of the achievable welfare gain at low revenue cost.
methodology: Structural model estimated on large transaction data plus an independent stated-preference survey of tipping preferences.
why_it_matters: Offers a transferable structural approach for evaluating how many preset levels to offer and where to place them—directly relevant to deciding whether 1x/2x/5x is the right menu or whether adding another preset level would help more users reach their true preference.
limitations: Tipping decisions on taxi rides, not financial savings, so magnitudes will differ.
No enrollment or persistence measures relevant to a savings feature.
relevance_reason: The structural decomposition of default adherence into deviation and opt-out costs, and the counterfactual menu-design analysis, are the specific technique that transfers to deciding how many preset multiplier levels to offer.

key_finding: An opt-in short-term liquid savings account offered via payroll deduction at five UK firms saw only 0.7% of eligible employees ever activate it, but among those who did, 96% still had a balance and 87% received a contribution at month 12.
methodology: Field study of program introduction and take-up across five UK employers, tracking activation and 12-month account activity.
why_it_matters: Directly informs the opt-in-vs-default choice: shows opt-in alone yields almost no enrollment even for a genuinely liquid, withdrawable savings product, while retention among those who opt in is excellent—suggesting the entry mechanism, not engagement, is the bottleneck opt-in fails to solve.
limitations: Enrollment is via employer payroll deduction, so the 'trusted employer intermediary' effect the brief says doesn't transfer to a banking app is present here.
Small employer sample (five UK firms).
relevance_reason: The closest available product analog to a round-up account (liquid, withdrawable, short-term) and directly quantifies opt-in's enrollment failure, though the employer-payroll channel limits direct transfer.

key_finding: Derives asymptotic characterizations of optimal default design, showing that when designer and choosers agree on an activity's value, simple opt-out-minimizing defaults are approximately optimal, with extensions for externalities and normative disagreement.
methodology: Theoretical/mathematical model of optimal default design verified with numerical simulations; abstract-only, no field data.
why_it_matters: Offers a general decision-theoretic framework for when a single default (e.g., a pre-set multiplier) is optimal versus when disagreement about value calls for a different design—useful for reasoning about the level decision even without app-specific data.
limitations: Purely theoretical with simulated verification, no empirical test in any consumer setting.
Abstract does not specify a financial-product application.
relevance_reason: A general theory of optimal default design applicable in principle to the preset-multiplier decision, though it offers no empirical effect sizes for our setting.

key_finding: Maps EU laws on dark patterns onto a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations, framing regulation of pre-selected defaults and similar choice-architecture tactics as protection of consumer autonomy rather than pure welfare.
methodology: Legal doctrinal analysis and taxonomy-building across EU consumer-protection statutes; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the legal test for whether our opt-out default or pre-set multiplier would read as a dark pattern under EU law, directly bearing on which entry mechanism is defensible, not just effective.
limitations: normative legal analysis, not an empirical study of enrolment or savings behaviour
no financial-product-specific case studies
framework, not measured effect sizes
relevance_reason: Directly addresses the EU dark-pattern/manipulation risk the brief flags as a reputational constraint on the opt-out design.

key_finding: At a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had not opted out after 12 months (versus ~50% at lower defaults in prior literature), and many stayed anchored at 12% despite it being financially suboptimal for them.
methodology: Administrative data analysis of a single employer retirement plan with an unusually high default; literature comparison for baseline opt-out rates.
why_it_matters: Shows a pre-set level can anchor people well past the point of financial sense, and that low-income employees are anchored more strongly — directly relevant to whether a pre-selected round-up multiplier will anchor rather than merely suggest.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer self-directed liquid savings product
no employer-as-intermediary control condition
relevance_reason: Strongest available evidence on anchoring at a pre-set contribution level, the mechanism behind C3, even though the setting is a pension plan.

key_finding: Abstract text was not usable (returned as a placeholder), so no quotable result is available; title indicates four large-scale UK field experiments on automated short-term (non-retirement) payroll savings.
methodology: abstract-only (content unavailable); appears to be multi-site UK field experiments by the same team behind other automatic-enrollment studies in this list.
why_it_matters: If the underlying experiments compare enrolment designs for short-term, liquid, automated savings rather than retirement, this is one of the closest analogues to a round-up feature — but the missing abstract means the actual findings cannot be weighed yet.
limitations: abstract content is missing/garbled, so no verifiable findings
payroll-based savings still involves an employer intermediary unlike a standalone banking app
relevance_reason: Title suggests a near-perfect analogue (short-term liquid savings automation, UK, multiple large experiments) but content could not be assessed.

key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrolment into just-in-time overdraft alerts reduces unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, worth an estimated £170-240 million annually market-wide, though alerts capture less than half of the achievable savings.
methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments at major UK retail banks comparing automatic enrolment into alert types.
why_it_matters: This is a consumer banking auto-enrolment feature at the same institutions and scale as ours, giving a real effect-size benchmark for what auto-enrolment can deliver in a live app, and evidence that even a working default captures only part of the possible benefit.
limitations: measures charge reduction, not savings-pot enrolment or amount saved
no explicit long-horizon (6-12 month) retention analysis reported in the abstract
alerts are a passive notification, not a savings-contribution decision
relevance_reason: Closest available consumer-banking evidence on auto-enrolment's real financial effect at scale, directly informing the entry-decision trade-off.

key_finding: In a large-scale UK natural experiment, automatic pension enrolment raised savings by £32-38/month but was partially offset by £7/month more unsecured debt and higher mortgage balances, even as defaults, over 41 months, modestly improved credit scores and reduced defaults.
methodology: Randomized roll-out of automatic enrolment pensions across ~160,000 UK employers with 2-29 employees, tracked over 41 months.
why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the assumption that a higher enrolment number equals a real savings gain — some of the nominal saving is financed by more debt, which is exactly the 'vanity enrolment' risk the support team is raising.
limitations: employer-sponsored pension, not a self-directed consumer savings app
locked, illiquid retirement savings rather than liquid round-up pots
relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that default-driven savings increases are a clean welfare win, a core question the brief poses.

key_finding: Adding a minor enrolment 'ordeal' (removing auto-enrolment) to health insurance reduced enrolment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Natural experiment around removal of an auto-enrolment policy in a health insurance market, with a theoretical selection model.
why_it_matters: Quantifies how large the enrolment cost of removing a default (or requiring active choice) can be, and shows it falls hardest on disadvantaged groups — a direct data point for the distributional question the brief asks about who is helped or hurt.
limitations: health insurance selection market, not a consumer financial savings product
adverse-selection dynamics specific to insurance don't map directly onto a savings pot
relevance_reason: Gives a concrete, large effect size for default removal plus explicit distributional harm, relevant to C1 and C5 despite the different market.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults raised campaign donations by over $43 million but also increased requested refunds by almost $3 million, with the largest effects on smaller, less-experienced donors who apparently did not intend the recurring commitment.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting different rollout timing of pre-checked recurring-donation boxes across U.S. political campaign websites.
why_it_matters: The pre-checked recurring-payment mechanism is structurally identical to a default-on round-up multiplier: it shows the same default can lift the headline number while creating unintended recurring commitments and complaint-like behaviour (refund requests) concentrated among the least experienced users.
limitations: political donations, not a savings or banking product
refund requests are a proxy for regret, not a direct measure of savings withdrawal or complaints
relevance_reason: Directly demonstrates the 'nominal enrolment vs genuine intent' failure mode the support team worries about, via a near-identical checkbox-default mechanism.

key_finding: In lab experiments, a default option raises the reservation utility that triggers search, both by shifting reference points and via self-selection of higher-aspiration searchers into active search.
methodology: Laboratory search experiments testing a reference-dependent search model with and without a default option.
why_it_matters: Offers a general behavioural mechanism (reference effects on search) but says nothing about enrolment persistence, savings amounts, or financial-product settings, so it does not move either design decision much.
limitations: abstract general-search lab task, not a financial or enrolment decision
no consumer financial product context
no measure of amount saved or persistence
relevance_reason: Tangential theoretical mechanism about defaults and search; included for completeness but low actionability.

key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects still present 15 months after rollout.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design around staggered EU Digital Markets Act choice-screen rollout across iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: This is the most direct evidence available that a forced active-choice screen produces large, persistent behaviour change in an EU-regulated mobile app context — exactly the comparison the active-choice design option needs before it's chosen over opt-out.
limitations: mobile browser choice, not a financial savings decision
platform differences (iOS vs Android rollout) complicate attributing the full effect to the choice screen alone
relevance_reason: Best available real-world evidence on active/forced choice screens under the same EU regulatory regime the product operates in, central to the C6 question.

key_finding: In a usability study of 410 participants, generalizable active-choice opt-out interfaces (e.g., choosing website categories) cut felt disruption from opting out, with 98% of participants reporting no disruption for the least-disruptive scheme versus a 40-point-lower baseline.
methodology: Design and usability study of nine privacy opt-out interface schemes implemented as a browser extension, tested with 410 participants.
why_it_matters: Shows that active-choice interfaces can be made low-friction without defaults, informing how an active-choice onboarding screen for the round-up feature could be designed to avoid feeling burdensome.
limitations: privacy opt-out context, not financial enrolment
no measure of downstream financial behaviour or engagement
relevance_reason: Relevant methods contribution on making active-choice interfaces usable, a design lever for the active-choice option.

key_finding: Switching university exam sign-up to opt-out increased sign-up in both single- and multi-exam settings, but improved actual task completion only for the single-exam case and only among individuals already responsive to the institution, with no gains for non-responsive individuals.
methodology: Two field experiments changing exam sign-up defaults to opt-out and tracking sign-up, participation, and pass rates.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the brief's central worry: a default can lift the headline enrolment number while doing nothing for the effortful behaviour that actually matters (continued round-up contributions), and the benefit concentrates on people who would have engaged anyway.
limitations: university exam context, not a financial or savings decision
small number of study programs, limited generalizability
relevance_reason: Best available analogue for whether nominal opt-out enrolment translates into effortful, sustained engagement — the core persistence question (C2, C5).

key_finding: After target-date funds became a permitted default investment option, younger and older workers' stock allocations diverged in line with the fund's glidepath, but contribution rates changed little.
methodology: Account-level panel data on millions of U.S. middle-class investors, 2006-2018, exploiting the Pension Protection Act's effect on default investment options.
why_it_matters: Suggests a preset default can strongly shape allocation/composition choices while leaving the underlying contribution level largely untouched, a useful caution that a preset multiplier might anchor 'which tier' without changing overall commitment much.
limitations: employer retirement plan and asset allocation, not a consumer round-up savings level
does not directly study enrolment or contribution-level anchoring
relevance_reason: Weak but relevant analogy for whether a preset option anchors composition versus amount, an open question for the multiplier design.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT on voluntary pension saving in China, all tested nudges — including default options — significantly reduced willingness to contribute relative to control, contrary to prevailing international evidence, with the largest backfire effects for positive-narrative and default-option nudges.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the brief's stated internal premise that 'defaults will lift enrolment' by showing a default option can backfire and reduce willingness to contribute, with effects varying by income, education, and gender — exactly the heterogeneity the brief wants surfaced before committing to opt-out.
limitations: small online-survey sample (n=220), not a live financial product
Chinese cultural/institutional context may not transfer to an EU consumer app
self-reported willingness rather than observed enrolment or savings behaviour
relevance_reason: One of the few papers in this set that directly contradicts the 'defaults always help' premise the brief explicitly asks to test.

key_finding: Across 36 hypothetical financial-intervention scenarios with 2,100 Australians, people generally approve of financial nudges, prefer System 2 (deliberative) framings and savings-framed interventions, and transparency does not reduce approval.
methodology: Pre-registered online survey experiment varying transparency, framing, and System-1/2 targeting across 36 scenarios; six dependent variables including manipulation ratings.
why_it_matters: Directly informs the reputational/dark-pattern risk question: shows consumers broadly do not perceive savings-framed, deliberative financial nudges as manipulative, which supports pursuing an opt-out or active-choice design over an opt-in-only one, provided it is framed around saving rather than spending.
limitations: hypothetical scenarios rather than an actual product experience
Australian sample, not EU
does not measure enrollment or amount effects, only attitudes
relevance_reason: Provides direct evidence on when a financial default/nudge is perceived as helpful versus manipulative, the C5 question central to the EU reputational-risk constraint.

key_finding: Offering CCT beneficiaries a choice of bank-account delivery had no significant average effect on savings, but increased balances specifically for individuals who previously held nonpositive balances.
methodology: Field experiment among conditional cash transfer beneficiaries comparing cash versus bank-account delivery of transfers.
why_it_matters: Suggests default account-based delivery mainly helps those starting from zero, a mild data point for who benefits from automatic mechanisms, but the mechanism (transfer delivery choice) is not an enrollment default.
limitations: low-income CCT beneficiaries in a developing-country context, not a consumer banking app user
not about opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrollment design
no persistence data beyond the study window
relevance_reason: Touches on heterogeneous savings benefits of account-based defaults but is a different mechanism (transfer delivery) and population than the brief's setting.

key_finding: Compares scenarios of a universal automatic IRA with an emergency (liquid) savings component, noting contribution amounts and liquid-fund availability do not differ across cases described.
methodology: abstract-only; appears to be a policy/simulation comparison of automatic IRA program designs with an emergency savings feature.
why_it_matters: The pairing of automatic enrollment with a liquid emergency-savings sleeve is structurally close to a round-up feature, but the abstract is too fragmentary to extract usable effect sizes for the enrollment or level decisions.
limitations: abstract is garbled/incomplete, no clear findings extractable
auto-IRA context still involves payroll/state-mediated enrollment, not a self-directed banking app
no citation count or venue信息 to assess rigor
relevance_reason: Closest analogue found to a liquid, auto-enrolled savings vehicle, but data quality from the abstract is too poor to be actionable.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment with a default contribution rate and fund dramatically raised participation, and most enrollees stuck to the default rate and fund even years later, describing this as the 'power of suggestion.'
methodology: Before/after administrative-data comparison of one large U.S. corporation's 401(k) participation under opt-in versus automatic enrollment.
why_it_matters: This is the canonical result the internal 'defaults will lift enrollment' argument rests on; it also demonstrates strong anchoring on the default rate, which is exactly the risk the pre-set multiplier decision needs to guard against.
limitations: employer-mediated 401(k) plan, so the trusted-intermediary mechanism the brief flags as non-transferable is present
2001 data predating app-based fintech and EU regulatory context
no data on withdrawal or disengagement of passively enrolled savers
relevance_reason: The foundational pension automatic-enrollment study the brief explicitly says newer work must be measured against, given the employer-intermediary caveat.

key_finding: No usable finding available; abstract is missing.
methodology: abstract-only; title indicates a comparison of savings behaviors between automatic and voluntary enrollment in a defined contribution retirement plan.
why_it_matters: Could add another automatic-vs-voluntary enrollment comparison, but with no abstract there is nothing to weigh against the brief's decisions.
limitations: no abstract provided, so findings, methodology, and effect sizes are unknown
employer defined-contribution plan setting, off the brief's consumer-app target
very recent/forthcoming, unreviewed by citations
relevance_reason: Title suggests direct relevance to enrollment-design comparison but the record carries no extractable content.

key_finding: Limited institutional trust and non-national minority status are both associated with under-saving and with early withdrawal from a mandatory pension scheme once early withdrawal was permitted, indicating a 'double jeopardy' for already-vulnerable savers.
methodology: Analysis of three representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) around a pension-freedom reform that introduced an early-withdrawal option.
why_it_matters: Directly warns that giving people freedom to exit (analogous to an opt-out) can concentrate harm on low-trust, minority populations who already save least, which is central to the brief's distributional/heterogeneity question (C5) and to the risk of a defaulted-in feature that some groups quietly drain.
limitations: mandatory state pension context, not a self-directed consumer app
Estonia-specific institutional and demographic context
no data on amounts saved or enrollment defaults per se, only withdrawal decisions
relevance_reason: Strong evidence on who is helped versus hurt by savings-scheme design changes, matching the brief's demand for distributional analysis.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, prompting people to reflect on being automatically enrolled into a vaccination-booster default reduced their stated intention to get boosted and reduced approval of the default policy itself, rather than reinforcing it.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment across G7 countries manipulating reflection on a hypothetical default-enrollment policy.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults straightforwardly help: reflecting on being auto-enrolled can trigger backlash and lower approval, a warning sign for a default-in round-up feature that becomes visible or scrutinized (e.g., via support complaints or media coverage).
limitations: vaccination/public-health policy setting, not financial products
hypothetical policy vignette rather than an actual product experience
no data on actual enrollment behavior, only stated intentions and approval
relevance_reason: Provides the brief's requested contradicting evidence that defaults can backfire once users reflect on being auto-enrolled, relevant to the reputational and manipulation-perception concerns.

key_finding: Using 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study data, automatic enrollment and employer contributions are associated with higher likelihood of retirement-plan participation among Millennials, while their absence explains much non-participation.
methodology: Cross-sectional survey analysis controlling for debt, income, risk tolerance, and assets.
why_it_matters: Reconfirms the standard default-raises-participation finding in yet another employer-plan sample, adding little beyond what Madrian & Shea and Chetty et al already establish for this brief's purposes.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan with employer matching, the exact intermediary mechanism the brief says doesn't transfer
cross-sectional, no persistence or withdrawal data
no distributional or anchoring analysis
relevance_reason: Another confirmatory employer-plan automatic-enrollment study; adds confirmation but no new mechanism relevant to the consumer app decision.

key_finding: Using 41 million observations in Denmark, each $1 of government subsidy expenditure raised total saving by only 1 cent because 85% of people are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but heavily moved by automatic (default) employer contributions, while the 15% 'active savers' who do respond are wealthier and more sophisticated.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data analysis of Danish retirement savings accounts, decomposing active versus passive responses to subsidies and automatic contributions.
why_it_matters: Gives the clearest quantified evidence that passive/default mechanisms move a very different (less sophisticated) population than active mechanisms move, directly informing the brief's concern about who is helped by defaults versus who was already going to save.
limitations: Danish retirement/tax-advantaged savings accounts, an employer/government-mediated setting
measures long-run wealth shifting across account types rather than liquid, discretionary round-up saving
predates app-based fintech and current EU dark-pattern scrutiny
relevance_reason: The strongest available evidence on heterogeneity between active and passive savers under default versus subsidy-based mechanisms, central to the brief's distributional question even though set in retirement accounts.

key_finding: Introduces and field-tests 'enhanced active choice,' a forced-choice design that highlights the losses of the non-preferred option, as an alternative to opt-out defaults when automatic enrollment is infeasible or ethically fraught, building on prior active-choice work in savings behavior.
methodology: Review of prior active-choice literature plus a series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice.
why_it_matters: Speaks directly to whether active choice can capture most of the enrollment benefit of a default without the ethical/manipulation cost, and offers a concrete design variant (loss-framed active choice) the team could test instead of choosing purely opt-in/opt-out/active-choice as equal alternatives.
limitations: primary field experiments are in medication adherence, not financial products
savings-behavior discussion is drawn from prior literature review rather than this paper's own new financial data
no 6-12 month persistence data reported
relevance_reason: The paper most directly on point for the entry-mechanism decision, proposing and testing active-choice designs explicitly as an alternative to defaults, including in the context of savings behavior.

key_finding: Synthesizes household-finance behavioral evidence across savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance, and reviews interventions including choice architecture, product design, and disclosure that firms and governments use to shape financial outcomes.
methodology: Narrative review/overview chapter (NBER) synthesizing the behavioral household finance literature.
why_it_matters: The broad synthesis of choice-architecture effects across consumer financial products (not employer plans specifically) the brief asked for as a review giving effect sizes rather than a single study, useful for calibrating expectations about the round-up feature's design levers generally.
limitations: a narrative overview, not a systematic review or meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
covers many financial domains, so savings-specific and app-specific detail is diluted
2018 publication, predating the newest fintech default-design literature
relevance_reason: Best available broad review of choice-architecture interventions in consumer (not solely employer) financial behavior, satisfying the brief's request for synthesis-level evidence.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of enrollees initially accepted both the default 2-3% contribution rate and default conservative fund, and half still did so after three years, largely offsetting the wealth gains from higher participation.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large U.S. firms comparing pre- and post-automatic-enrollment cohorts.
why_it_matters: The definitive demonstration that a pre-set default level anchors most users for years, directly warning that shipping a pre-selected round-up multiplier risks anchoring people below what they would otherwise choose, and that enrollment gains can be offset by anchoring effects on amount.
limitations: 401(k) employer plan with an intermediary employer relationship the brief says doesn't transfer
2001 data, predating app-based product design and EU rules
measures retirement contribution/investment defaults, not a liquid round-up multiplier
relevance_reason: The foundational study on default-level anchoring persistence, the exact risk the brief's second design decision (pre-set multiplier) needs evidence on.

key_finding: In a randomized experiment on salary-linked savings accounts in Afghanistan, default enrollment raised participation by 40 percentage points (equivalent to a 50% matching incentive), driven mainly by present bias and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios, and it also increased later active decisions to save after the study ended.
methodology: Randomized field experiment assigning employees to different salary-linked savings account default conditions, with follow-up mechanism-testing interventions.
why_it_matters: Explains why defaults work (inertia/cognitive cost rather than genuine preference) and shows the effect can persist into subsequent active choice, which bears on whether a defaulted-in round-up feature would produce durable engagement or just nominal enrollment that later disengages.
limitations: salary-linked, employer-mediated account rather than a fully self-directed consumer banking app
Afghan employee population, very different economic and regulatory context from EU consumers
no data on withdrawal, complaints, or amount saved over 6-12 months
relevance_reason: Offers rare causal evidence on the mechanism behind the default effect and its persistence into active saving, informing whether passive enrollment risk of disengagement is likely.

key_finding: A randomized reminder intervention on a Brazilian financial platform cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised checking-account overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Field experiment (randomized reminder nudge) with a consumer financial management platform in Brazil, comparing fee outcomes across credit card and checking account products.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the support team's worry: a well-intentioned nudge can help most users while making a defined subgroup worse off, which is exactly the distributional check the brief wants before defaulting everyone into round-up savings.
limitations: Studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or contribution-level anchors
Credit card/overdraft fee context rather than a round-up savings pot
Brazilian credit market may differ from EU consumer-protection context
relevance_reason: Best available evidence in this shortlist that a helpful-seeming nudge can produce net harm for an identifiable user segment, bearing directly on C5's who-is-helped/who-is-hurt question.
